passage: Clinic note by Dr Mehak. Disha (5) came in gripping her father's hand and hiding her face in his sleeve. I said hello, kept my voice low, and held up the stethoscope. "This is a listening tool. Do you want to hear your own heart first?" She peeked, then nodded. I put the ear pieces in her ears and the round end on her chest. Her eyes grew wide. "It goes thump-thump!" she whispered. After that she sat up and let me listen to her chest too. She asked if she could listen to Papa's heart next, and I said yes.

qa.q: What did Dr Mehak let Disha listen to first?
qa.a: Dr Mehak let Disha listen to her own heart.

qa.q: How did Disha feel when she heard the thump-thump?
qa.a: Disha felt curious and less afraid. Her wide eyes and asking to listen to Papa's heart next show it.

qa.q: What did the doctor do that helped Disha trust her?
qa.a: She spoke kindly, showed the stethoscope, and let Disha use it, so Disha was included in what happened. Being included helps a child feel brave. 🙂

qa.q: How might Disha's father feel watching his daughter with the doctor?
qa.a: He may feel relieved to see his daughter calm. He held her hand at the start and may now feel more sure about the doctor.

grounding: A doctor speaks kindly, shows the stethoscope and lets the child listen, so the child is less afraid, curious, and trusting.

passage: In the clinic waiting room, Uma lay on the bench with her head on Mummy's lap. A nurse brought her a cup of juice, and someone gave her a sticker. Pankaj sat on the hard chair with his arms folded. "She gets everything," he muttered. His chest felt tight and hot. "I want to be ill too." Mummy heard him. She reached over and squeezed his hand. "Uma needs rest to get better. You and I will read your dinosaur book tonight, just us." Pankaj looked at the floor, then slowly leaned against her shoulder.

qa.q: What did Uma get from the nurse and someone else?
qa.a: A nurse brought her a cup of juice, and someone gave her a sticker.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he said "I want to be ill too"?
qa.a: Pankaj felt jealous and left out, because Uma was getting the care and treats. His tight, hot chest and folded arms show it.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Pankaj, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Mummy squeezed his hand, explained that Uma needs rest, and promised a special reading time just for him. This gives him care of his own so he does not need to be sick to get attention. 🙂

qa.q: How might Uma feel about all the attention she is getting?
qa.a: Uma probably feels unwell and tired and wants to be held. She might not notice Pankaj's feelings at all.

grounding: A child whose sibling is sick feels jealous and wishes he were sick too, and a wise parent gives him some care time and explains the sick child needs rest.

passage: Abebe's forehead felt hot, and his tummy hurt. He lay curled on the sofa in Addis Ababa with his fists wrapped in Mummy's scarf. When Yara stood up to stir the soup, he cried, "Don't go!" and grabbed her hand with both of his. He felt afraid and small. Yara sat back down and stroked his cheek. "I'm only going to the kitchen. Look, you can see me from here. I will be back when the soup is bubbling, and you can call if you need me." Abebe nodded, still holding one corner of her scarf.

qa.q: Where was Abebe lying?
qa.a: Abebe was lying on the sofa in Addis Ababa.

qa.q: What was Abebe feeling when he cried "Don't go!"?
qa.a: Abebe was afraid and felt helpless because he was ill. Clinging to Yara's hand was his way of asking for safety.

qa.q: How did Yara respond in a helpful way?
qa.a: Yara told him where she was going, that he could see her, and when she would be back. She did not call him naughty for clinging.

qa.q: How might Yara feel as her son holds her hand?
qa.a: Yara may feel tender and worried, and torn between the soup and staying beside him. She was willing to sit back down first.

grounding: A sick child clings to his mother and does not want her to leave, feels afraid and helpless, and she stays close and tells him when she will be back.

passage:
"Amma, where is Bruno?" Charu stood at the door, holding his red leash.
"Sit with me, kanna," said Lavanya. "I have sad news. Bruno died. His body stopped working, and he can't come back."
"But where did he go?"
"He is not in his body anymore. It's true, and I'm sad too."
Charu's face crumpled and she cried loudly. Lavanya held her. "You can cry as long as you need."
Later Charu asked for crayons. "I'm drawing Bruno. To say goodbye."

qa.q: What was Charu holding at the door?
qa.a: Charu was holding Bruno's red leash.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she asked where Bruno had gone?
qa.a: Charu felt sad and confused, like a big empty hole. She asked where he went because she did not yet understand that he cannot come back.

qa.q: How did Lavanya help Charu with her grief?
qa.a: She told the truth in simple words, let Charu cry as long as she needed, and later let her draw a goodbye.

qa.q: How might Lavanya be feeling as she tells Charu about Bruno?
qa.a: Lavanya is sad too, as she said, and may find it hard to say the words. She stays close and honest so Charu is not alone.

grounding: A child cries and asks where her dog has gone, and wise adults tell the truth simply, allow crying and let her draw a goodbye.

passage: I'm Neelam, their neighbour. Yesterday I was hanging washing on the balcony when I heard Swati crying next door. Their dog had died in the morning. Her father Yogesh sat on the floor and pulled her into a hug. He said quietly, "It is okay to be sad. We loved him very much." He did not say to stop crying, and he did not mention getting a new dog. Swati pushed her face into his shirt and her shoulders shook. I can't know exactly what she felt, but she stayed there a long time.

qa.q: Who was crying, and what had happened?
qa.a: Swati was crying because the family's dog had died in the morning.

qa.q: What might Swati have been feeling as she stayed in her father's arms?
qa.a: Swati may have felt understood as well as sad. Neelam cannot know for sure, but Swati pushed her face into his shirt and stayed a long time.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do that let Swati's grief take its natural path?
qa.a: He hugged her and told her it is okay to be sad because they loved him, and he did not tell her to stop crying or to get a new dog. 🤍

qa.q: How might Yogesh be feeling as he sits on the floor with Swati?
qa.a: Yogesh probably misses the dog too, since he said "We loved him very much." He seems to put Swati's sadness first.

grounding: A parent hugs a grieving child, saying it is okay to be sad because they loved the dog, without telling her to stop crying or replace him, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Moti the cat died in the night, and Mummy Harsha told Uday over breakfast in their flat. He put his spoon down. Yesterday he had forgotten to fill Moti's bowl, and last week he had shouted, "I hate you, Moti!" when the cat scratched his hand. Uday's stomach twisted. "Mummy, I made him die," he whispered. "Because I was bad." Harsha pulled him onto her lap. "Listen to me. It was not because of anything you did. Not the bowl, not the shouting. Moti got very old and his body stopped working." Uday sniffed and held her sleeve.

qa.q: What did Uday forget to do for Moti yesterday?
qa.a: Uday forgot to fill Moti's bowl.

qa.q: What did Uday think had caused Moti's death?
qa.a: Uday thought his own actions, forgetting the bowl and shouting at Moti, had made the cat die. His twisted stomach and whisper show how guilty and frightened he felt.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that helped Uday?
qa.a: Harsha said clearly that it was not because of anything he did and named the things he was worrying about. She then gave a simple honest reason and held him.

qa.q: How might Harsha be feeling as Uday says he made Moti die?
qa.a: Harsha may feel sorry that he is carrying this guilt, and sad about Moti as well. She acts quickly to lift the blame off him.

grounding: A child believes it is his fault the cat died because he forgot to feed him and was angry, and a wise adult says clearly it was not because of anything he did.

passage: Counsellor's note by Irfan. Diya's rabbit died on Sunday. On Monday at the school gate she was crying, and her brother Abhinav stood next to her, very quiet, rubbing his eyes. He told me, "I'm sad because Diya is sad." They hugged for a long time. I did not tell them to stop or say it would be fine. I asked if they would like to do something for the rabbit. They chose to plant a marigold by the school wall. Both dug the hole, and Abhinav patted the soil flat.

qa.q: What did Diya and Abhinav plant by the school wall?
qa.a: They planted a marigold.

qa.q: How did Abhinav feel as he watched his sister cry?
qa.a: Abhinav felt sad because Diya was sad. He said so himself, and he stood quiet and rubbed his eyes.

qa.q: Why did planting the flower help the children?
qa.a: It gave them something to do together and a way to remember the rabbit. Sharing sadness with a sibling and having a small ritual helps both of them. 🤍

qa.q: How might Diya feel with Abhinav beside her?
qa.a: Diya may feel less alone in her grief. He hugged her for a long time and helped dig, so she knows he shares her sadness.

grounding: A child feels sad watching his sister cry for the pet and they hold each other, and a counsellor suggests planting a flower as a way to remember.

passage: At circle time in the school hall, Bhupen said quietly that his dog had died. Ritu shrugged. "It's just a dog. You can get another one." Bhupen's throat went tight and his eyes stung. He looked at his shoes. "He was my friend," he said. Ritu blinked and said nothing. After circle, the teacher, Ms Alka, knelt near them. "Ritu, when a friend loses a pet, we can say, 'I'm sorry about your dog.' Let's practise." Ritu said it. Bhupen nodded, still sad, but his shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What did Ritu say when Bhupen told the group about his dog?
qa.a: Ritu said, "It's just a dog. You can get another one."

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after Ritu's words?
qa.a: Bhupen felt hurt and misunderstood. His tight throat and stinging eyes show it, and he answered, "He was my friend."

qa.q: How did Ms Alka help both children?
qa.a: She taught Ritu gentle words to say to a friend who lost a pet and had her practise them. Bhupen also got to hear kind words.

qa.q: Why might Ritu have said what she did?
qa.a: Ritu may not have known what to say, so she said the first thing she thought. Her blink and silence suggest she had not thought about how it would land.

grounding: A child whose dog died is told it is just a dog, feels hurt and says he was my friend, and a teacher teaches gentle words.

passage: Jyoti sat on the empty charpai in the courtyard, where Nani used to tell her stories about the clever crow. Nani had died two days ago. Jyoti touched the folded blanket and her eyes filled. "Mummy, where is Nani? Is she cold?" Rehana sat beside her. "Nani died, Jyoti. Her body stopped working and she cannot come back. I miss her too." The next morning Jyoti asked again, "Where is Nani?" Rehana answered the same way and took out a photo. "Look, here she is with you. Shall I tell the crow story the way she did?"

qa.q: Where did Jyoti sit?
qa.a: Jyoti sat on the empty charpai in the courtyard.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she asked, "Is she cold?"
qa.a: Jyoti felt sad and confused, missing her Nani and her stories and not knowing where she was. She touched the blanket, as if looking for her.

qa.q: How did Rehana respond in a wise way to Jyoti's repeated question?
qa.a: She used simple honest words, answered again the next day without getting impatient, and kept Nani's memory alive with a photo and a story.

qa.q: How might Rehana be feeling as she answers Jyoti's questions?
qa.a: Rehana is grieving her own mother, since Jyoti's Nani is her mother, and said she missed her too. It may be hard, but she stays close.

grounding: A child misses her Nani and is confused about where she is, and a wise adult uses simple honest words, allows repeated questions, and keeps the memory alive with a photo and story.

passage:
Keerthana stood at the bedroom door in her socks. Papa was sitting on the bed with his hands over his face, and his shoulders were shaking.
"Papa?" she whispered.
Sahil wiped his eyes. "Come here, kanna."
"Why are you crying? Did I do something?"
"No. I'm sad because I miss Dadi. It is okay to be sad. I'm still here for you."
She climbed up and leaned against him. "I miss Dadi too," she said, very small.

qa.q: Where was Keerthana standing when she saw her father?
qa.a: Keerthana was standing at the bedroom door in her socks.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling as she watched her father cry?
qa.a: Keerthana was worried and scared. Her whisper and her question, "Did I do something?" show she wondered if it was her fault.

qa.q: How did Sahil's words help Keerthana?
qa.a: He said why he was crying, that it is okay to be sad, and that he was still there for her. Naming his grief kept her from fearing her own. 🤍

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Keerthana says she misses Dadi too?
qa.a: Sahil may feel comforted that they share the loss and that she can tell him. He may also feel tender towards her.

grounding: A child sees her father crying after Dadi died and feels worried, and he says he is sad because he misses Dadi, it is okay to be sad and he is still there.
